entries.lesson_core_move: Convert a cosine A cos(omega t + phi) into the phasor A angle phi, preserving amplitude and phase for same-frequency phasor addition.

sections.section_title: Introduction to Phasor Representation of a Cosine
sections.learning_goal: Define the cosine-to-phasor map as $A\cos(\omega t+\phi) \mapsto A\angle\phi$ and explain that the shared angular frequency is tracked separately for later same-frequency addition.

image_policy.image_description_seed: No image needed; the lesson is a symbolic conversion from cosine notation to phasor notation.
image_policy.image_generation_notes: Do not generate a visual. Keep this tutorial purely symbolic and notation-based.

question_policy.answer_format: not-applicable
question_policy.practice_question_model: not-applicable

tutorial_outline.direct_instruction_goal: Teach the base mapping from a single cosine to its phasor form: preserve amplitude, convert phase to the phasor angle, and keep the shared $\omega$ outside the phasor.
tutorial_outline.base_case: Start with the simplest cosine $A\cos(\omega t)$ and represent it as $A\angle 0$ before adding any phase shift.
paragraph_plan: Introduce the phasor convention and state that a cosine is represented by a magnitude-angle pair, not by the full time expression.
Show the base case $A\cos(\omega t)$ and map it to $A\angle 0$ so the learner sees that zero phase becomes a zero angle.
Generalize to $A\cos(\omega t+\phi)$ and show that the phase shift becomes the phasor angle while the amplitude stays unchanged.
Close by connecting the representation to later same-frequency addition: the common angular frequency is shared by all terms and is not part of the phasor value.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: not-applicable
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: not-applicable
example_outline.variation_from_previous: not-applicable

sections.handoff_notes: Keep the first pass compact: define the phasor mapping, show the zero-phase base case, then generalize to $A\angle\phi$ without introducing image data or extra algebra.

sections.section_title: Writing a Zero-Phase Cosine as a Phasor
sections.learning_goal: Translate a zero-phase cosine $A\cos(\omega t)$ into the phasor $A\angle 0$.

image_policy.image_description_seed: No image needed; the example is a direct symbolic conversion from cosine form to phasor form.
image_policy.image_generation_notes: Do not generate an image. Keep the worked example and the follow-up practice symbolic.

question_policy.answer_format: Choose the phasor $A\angle\phi$ that matches the given cosine.
question_policy.practice_question_model: What is the phasor form of $6\cos(\omega t)$?
distractor_plan: Use the time-domain cosine instead of a phasor.
Swap amplitude and phase or attach a nonzero phase angle.
Change the angle sign even though the phase is zero.
Insert $\omega t$ into the phasor expression.

tutorial_outline.direct_instruction_goal: not-applicable

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: Convert $6\cos(\omega t)$ into phasor form.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Show that a zero-phase cosine keeps the same amplitude and becomes the phasor $6\angle 0$.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: This is the first concrete conversion after the tutorial: the phase is zero, so the only task is to preserve the amplitude and write angle $0$.
solution_step_plan: Identify the amplitude as $6$.
Notice that the phase shift is $0$.
Write the phasor as $6\angle 0$.
Check that the shared $\omega$ is not copied into the phasor value.
practice_variation_axes: Amplitude only
Zero phase only
No frequency distraction

sections.handoff_notes: Use one clean symbolic conversion and keep the distractors focused on the three common errors: dropping amplitude, misreading zero phase, or copying the time factor into the phasor.

sections.section_title: Writing a Positive-Phase Cosine as a Phasor
sections.learning_goal: Translate a cosine with positive phase into a phasor by preserving the amplitude and writing the phase as the angle.

image_policy.image_description_seed: No image needed; the phase shift is read directly from the cosine and copied into the phasor angle.
image_policy.image_generation_notes: Do not generate a visual. The step is a symbolic phase-to-angle translation.

question_policy.answer_format: Choose the phasor $A\angle\phi$ that matches the given cosine.
question_policy.practice_question_model: What is the phasor form of $4\cos(\omega t+\pi/3)$?
distractor_plan: Flip the sign of the phase angle.
Omit the phase angle and keep only the amplitude.
Write the time-domain cosine instead of phasor form.
Swap the amplitude and phase positions.

tutorial_outline.direct_instruction_goal: not-applicable

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: Convert $4\cos(\omega t+\pi/3)$ into phasor form.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Show that a positive phase is copied directly into the phasor angle, giving $4\angle\pi/3$.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: The amplitude-and-zero-phase pattern stays the same, but now the learner must carry a positive phase shift into the angle.
solution_step_plan: Identify the amplitude as $4$.
Read the phase shift as $+\pi/3$.
Write the phasor as $4\angle\pi/3$.
Check that the positive sign appears in the angle, not in the amplitude.
practice_variation_axes: Positive phase values
Amplitude changes
Fractions of $\pi$

sections.handoff_notes: Keep this example close to the zero-phase case so the only new idea is that a positive phase becomes the angle of the phasor.

sections.section_title: Writing a Negative-Phase Cosine as a Phasor
sections.learning_goal: Translate a cosine with negative phase into a phasor by preserving the amplitude and keeping the negative angle.

image_policy.image_description_seed: No image needed; the sign of the phase is visible in the cosine notation and transfers directly to the phasor angle.
image_policy.image_generation_notes: Do not generate a visual. Keep the step focused on sign preservation in symbolic notation.

question_policy.answer_format: Choose the phasor $A\angle\phi$ that matches the given cosine.
question_policy.practice_question_model: What is the phasor form of $10\cos(\omega t-\pi/6)$?
distractor_plan: Flip the negative phase to a positive angle.
Drop the phase angle entirely and keep only the amplitude.
Move the minus sign onto the amplitude instead of the angle.
Return the original cosine instead of a phasor.

tutorial_outline.direct_instruction_goal: not-applicable

solution_step_plan: Identify the amplitude as $10$.
Read the phase shift as $-\pi/6$.
Write the phasor as $10\angle-\pi/6$.
Check that the sign belongs to the angle, not to the amplitude.
practice_variation_axes: Negative phase values
Amplitude changes
Phase-sign preservation

sections.handoff_notes: Target the sign error explicitly: the correct answer keeps the negative phase in the angle while leaving the amplitude positive.

sections.section_title: Separating the Shared Angular Frequency from the Phasor
sections.learning_goal: Separate the shared angular frequency from the phasor so the phasor stores only amplitude and phase.

image_policy.image_description_seed: No image needed; the shared angular frequency is a symbolic parameter that stays outside the phasor value.
image_policy.image_generation_notes: Do not generate an image. Keep the worked example symbolic and emphasize the separation between frequency and phasor.

question_policy.answer_format: Choose the phasor $A\angle\phi$ and keep the shared angular frequency separate.
question_policy.practice_question_model: What is the phasor form of $12\cos(\omega_0 t-\pi/4)$?
distractor_plan: Include $\omega_0$ inside the phasor instead of keeping it separate.
Flip the phase sign or drop the phase entirely.
Replace the phasor with the original cosine expression.
Change the amplitude while preserving the angle.

tutorial_outline.direct_instruction_goal: not-applicable

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: Convert $12\cos(\omega_0 t-\pi/4)$ into phasor form and keep $\omega_0$ separate from the phasor value.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Show that the phasor is $12\angle-\pi/4$ while $\omega_0$ remains the shared angular frequency that is not part of the phasor.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: The cosine-to-phasor rule is the same, but the example makes the frequency split explicit so the learner sees what is preserved and what is carried separately.
solution_step_plan: Identify the amplitude as $12$.
Read the phase as $-\pi/4$.
Write the phasor as $12\angle-\pi/4$.
State that $\omega_0$ is shared across same-frequency terms and is not embedded in the phasor.
practice_variation_axes: Explicit shared angular frequency labels
Amplitude and phase values
Keeping $\omega_0$ outside the phasor

sections.handoff_notes: Use this final example to lock in the separation of concerns: the phasor holds amplitude and phase, while the shared angular frequency stays outside the phasor for later addition.

entries.lesson_core_move: Add same-frequency cosines by recognizing their common angular frequency, converting each cosine to its phasor, and summing the phasors as complex quantities.

sections.section_title: Introduction to Adding Same-Frequency Cosines
sections.learning_goal: Explain that same-frequency cosines are added by preserving the shared angular frequency, converting each term to a phasor, and summing the phasors as complex quantities.

image_policy.image_description_seed: No image needed; this lesson is a symbolic setup for same-frequency phasor addition.
image_policy.image_generation_notes: Do not generate a visual. Keep the tutorial purely symbolic and notation-based.

question_policy.answer_format: not-applicable
question_policy.practice_question_model: not-applicable

tutorial_outline.direct_instruction_goal: Teach the minimum effective procedure for same-frequency cosine addition: identify the shared $\omega$, convert each cosine to $A\angle\phi$, and add the phasors as complex numbers.
tutorial_outline.base_case: Start with the simplest pair $A\cos(\omega t)+B\cos(\omega t)$ so the only new move is phasor addition with a shared frequency.
paragraph_plan: State the lesson rule: same-frequency cosines are not added directly in the time domain; they are converted to phasors that share one angular frequency tag.
Show the zero-phase base case $A\cos(\omega t)+B\cos(\omega t)$ and map it to $A\angle 0 + B\angle 0$.
Generalize to $A_1\cos(\omega t+\phi_1)+A_2\cos(\omega t+\phi_2)$ and show the corresponding phasors $A_1\angle\phi_1 + A_2\angle\phi_2$.
Explain that the phasors are complex quantities, so the sum is ordinary complex addition, while the shared $\omega$ stays outside the phasor value.
Close by pointing forward: later steps will make the phasor sum more explicit, but this lesson's job is to recognize the shared frequency and set up the sum correctly.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: not-applicable
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: not-applicable
example_outline.variation_from_previous: not-applicable

sections.handoff_notes: Keep the tutorial strictly symbolic and keep the frequency split explicit: the phasor stores amplitude and phase, while the shared $\omega$ is only the tag that makes the sum valid.

sections.section_title: Recognizing a Common Angular Frequency
sections.learning_goal: Identify when two cosine terms share the same angular frequency and can be treated as one phasor-addition problem.

image_policy.image_description_seed: No image needed; the shared angular frequency is read directly from the cosine arguments.
image_policy.image_generation_notes: Do not generate a visual. This step is a symbolic frequency-matching task.

question_policy.answer_format: Choose the shared angular frequency that appears in both cosine arguments.
question_policy.practice_question_model: What is the common angular frequency in $4\cos(5t+\pi/6)+7\cos(5t-\pi/3)$?
distractor_plan: Use an amplitude value such as $4$ or $7$ as if it were the frequency.
Use a phase value such as $\pi/6$ or $\pi/3$ as if it were the frequency.
Claim the frequencies differ because the amplitudes or phases differ.
Read the coefficient of $t$ incorrectly by ignoring the shared value.

tutorial_outline.direct_instruction_goal: not-applicable

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: In $4\cos(5t+\pi/6)+7\cos(5t-\pi/3)$, identify the shared angular frequency and decide whether the terms can be combined as same-frequency phasors.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Show that both terms have the same $\omega=5$, so the pair is eligible for phasor addition.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: This is the first recognition step: the learner compares two cosine arguments instead of converting a single cosine.
solution_step_plan: Read the coefficient of $t$ in each cosine argument.
Compare the coefficients and confirm that both are $5$.
State that the shared angular frequency is $\omega=5$.
Note that different amplitudes and phase shifts do not prevent phasor addition.
practice_variation_axes: Shared angular frequency only
Different amplitudes
Different phase shifts
Frequency matching versus frequency mismatch

sections.handoff_notes: Make the recognition step explicit: the student should decide that the cosines share $\omega$ before any phasor conversion happens.

sections.section_title: Converting Each Cosine to a Phasor
sections.learning_goal: Convert each same-frequency cosine to its phasor without losing amplitude or phase information.

image_policy.image_description_seed: No image needed; the conversion is fully symbolic.
image_policy.image_generation_notes: Do not generate a visual. Keep the conversion step notation-based and frequency-preserving.

question_policy.answer_format: Choose the phasor-sum expression that matches the two cosine terms.
question_policy.practice_question_model: What is the phasor-sum form of $4\cos(5t+\pi/6)+7\cos(5t-\pi/3)$?
distractor_plan: Leave the answer in time-domain cosine form instead of phasor form.
Flip the sign of one phase angle.
Insert the shared $\omega$ inside the phasor value.
Change one amplitude or combine the terms before converting them.

tutorial_outline.direct_instruction_goal: not-applicable

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: Convert $4\cos(5t+\pi/6)+7\cos(5t-\pi/3)$ into a phasor-sum expression.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Show that the two cosines become $4\angle\pi/6 + 7\angle-\pi/3$, with the shared $5$ kept separate.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: The frequency match is already known; now the learner must translate each term into phasor notation without changing amplitude or phase.
solution_step_plan: Identify the amplitude and phase of the first cosine term.
Write the first phasor as $4\angle\pi/6$.
Identify the amplitude and phase of the second cosine term.
Write the second phasor as $7\angle-\pi/3$ and keep the shared $\omega=5$ outside the phasors.
practice_variation_axes: Different amplitude values
Positive and negative phase signs
Explicit shared angular frequency labels

sections.handoff_notes: Keep the frequency tag visible and do not simplify the phasor sum yet; the goal here is clean conversion of each cosine term.

sections.section_title: Forming the Resultant Phasor Sum
sections.learning_goal: Write the converted phasors as a single resultant complex sum and keep the addition in phasor form.

image_policy.image_description_seed: No image needed; the result is a complex sum of phasors, not a diagram-based task.
image_policy.image_generation_notes: Do not generate a visual. Keep the phasor-sum result symbolic and do not introduce rectangular decomposition yet.

question_policy.answer_format: Choose the resultant phasor-sum expression for the two converted phasors.
question_policy.practice_question_model: What is the resultant phasor-sum expression for $5\cos(3t)+5\cos(3t-\pi/2)$?
distractor_plan: Keep the answer in time-domain cosine form.
Convert only one of the two terms to phasor form.
Prematurely jump to rectangular form instead of leaving the phasors in sum form.
Change the phase sign on one term or alter one amplitude.

tutorial_outline.direct_instruction_goal: not-applicable

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: Form the resultant phasor sum for $5\cos(3t)+5\cos(3t-\pi/2)$.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Show that the two phasors are added as $5\angle 0 + 5\angle-\pi/2$ and that the result remains a complex sum for later evaluation.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: This step shifts from conversion to combination: the learner now treats the phasors as complex quantities that are added together.
solution_step_plan: Convert the two cosine terms to phasors if needed.
Write the phasors side by side with a plus sign.
State that the result is the resultant phasor sum.
Leave the expression in phasor form rather than decomposing it into rectangular components.
practice_variation_axes: Two-term phasor sums
Equal amplitudes
Quarter-cycle phase separation
No rectangular decomposition yet

sections.handoff_notes: Emphasize that the plus sign is ordinary complex addition, but keep the answer in phasor form so the rectangular-form lesson can handle the next layer of work.

sections.section_title: Adding More Than Two Same-Frequency Cosine Phasors
sections.learning_goal: Extend same-frequency phasor addition to three or more cosine terms.

image_policy.image_description_seed: No image needed; the task is to extend the same symbolic phasor-sum rule to more than two terms.
image_policy.image_generation_notes: Do not generate a visual. Keep the example as a longer symbolic sum with the same angular frequency.

question_policy.answer_format: Choose the phasor-sum expression that includes all three same-frequency cosines.
question_policy.practice_question_model: What is the phasor-sum form of $2\cos(7t)+3\cos(7t+\pi/4)+4\cos(7t-\pi/3)$?
distractor_plan: Drop one of the three terms from the sum.
Copy the wrong shared angular frequency.
Flip the sign on one phase angle.
Collapse the three amplitudes into one number without preserving phase information.

tutorial_outline.direct_instruction_goal: not-applicable

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: Convert $2\cos(7t)+3\cos(7t+\pi/4)+4\cos(7t-\pi/3)$ into one phasor-sum expression.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Show that all three terms share $\omega=7$ and become $2\angle 0 + 3\angle\pi/4 + 4\angle-\pi/3$.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: The same rule now applies to three terms instead of two, so the learner must carry the shared frequency through a longer sum without dropping any term.
solution_step_plan: Identify the common angular frequency in all three cosine terms.
Convert the zero-phase term to $2\angle 0$.
Convert the positive-phase term to $3\angle\pi/4$.
Convert the negative-phase term to $4\angle-\pi/3$ and write the full phasor sum.

Different amplitudes
All terms sharing one angular frequency

sections.handoff_notes: Use this final example to show that the same phasor-addition rule scales to more than two cosines while preserving every term and the shared $\omega$.

entries.lesson_title: Rectangular Form of a Phasor Sum
entries.lesson_core_move: Compute the rectangular-form phasor sum for same-frequency cosines by resolving each phasor into real and imaginary components and adding corresponding components.

sections.section_title: Introduction to Rectangular Form of a Phasor Sum
sections.learning_goal: Teach the componentwise rule for adding same-frequency phasors in rectangular form.

image_policy.image_description_seed: No image needed; the lesson stays in rectangular notation.
image_policy.image_generation_notes: Keep the tutorial symbolic; do not generate a complex-plane diagram.

question_policy.answer_format: No questions in the tutorial section.
question_policy.practice_question_model: None; tutorial only.

tutorial_outline.direct_instruction_goal: Show that a same-frequency phasor can be rewritten in rectangular form as $a+jb$, and that phasor sums are formed by adding the real parts and imaginary parts separately.
tutorial_outline.base_case: Start with two phasors whose rectangular parts are already visible, so the learner sees the addition rule before any harder arithmetic.
paragraph_plan: Connect the rectangular sum to the prior phasor representation lesson and state that the task is to keep the common $\omega$ fixed while combining the phasor components through rectangular coordinates.
Introduce the rectangular form $a+jb$ and define the real part as the horizontal component and the imaginary part as the vertical component.
Show the two-term rule: write $X_1 = a_1 + jb_1$ and $X_2 = a_2 + jb_2$, then add the real parts together and the imaginary parts together.
Emphasize bookkeeping: signs stay attached to their components, and the result remains rectangular until the next lesson converts it to polar form.
Generalize the same componentwise rule to three or more phasors so later examples can scale without changing the method.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: Not applicable; tutorial step.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Not applicable; tutorial step.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: Not applicable; tutorial step.

sections.handoff_notes: Keep the explanation symbolic and compact. Do not convert the sum to polar form in this section.

sections.section_title: Adding Axis-Aligned Phasor Components
sections.learning_goal: Add phasors that are already aligned with the real or imaginary axis by combining components directly.

image_policy.image_description_seed: No image needed; the arithmetic is purely symbolic.
image_policy.image_generation_notes: Keep the worked example and questions in rectangular notation only.

question_policy.answer_format: Five symbolic answer choices in rectangular form $a+jb$; choose the single correct sum.
question_policy.practice_question_model: What is the rectangular-form sum of $2 + j0$ and $0 + j4$?
distractor_plan: Swap the real and imaginary parts.
Add only the nonzero parts and forget the zero component.
Drop the $j$ and treat the components as ordinary scalars.
Turn the sum into a polar magnitude-angle form too early.

tutorial_outline.direct_instruction_goal: Not applicable; this is a worked example.
tutorial_outline.base_case: Not applicable; this is a worked example.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: Add the phasors $3 + j0$ and $0 + j5$ and write the result in rectangular form.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Show the simplest rectangular sum where one phasor is purely real and the other is purely imaginary.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: This is the first worked computation after the tutorial, and the phasors are already axis-aligned so the only new work is componentwise addition.
solution_step_plan: Rewrite each phasor with its real and imaginary parts visible.
Add the real parts together and keep the imaginary part from the second term.
Add the imaginary parts together and keep the real part from the first term.
State the final sum as a single $a+jb$ expression.
practice_variation_axes: Change the magnitudes of the real and imaginary axis terms.
Switch which phasor lies on the real axis and which lies on the imaginary axis.

sections.section_title: Resolving Two Cosine Phasors into Rectangular Components
sections.learning_goal: Resolve two same-frequency cosines into rectangular phasors and add their real and imaginary parts separately.

image_policy.image_description_seed: No image needed; the conversion and sum stay symbolic.

Use the wrong sign for the negative phase angle.
Add magnitudes instead of components.

tutorial_outline.direct_instruction_goal: Not applicable; this is a worked example.
tutorial_outline.base_case: Not applicable; this is a worked example.

entries.lesson_title: Polar Form of a Phasor Sum
entries.lesson_core_move: Convert a rectangular phasor sum into polar magnitude-angle form so the resultant sinusoid's amplitude and phase can be read from the phasor.

sections.section_title: Introduction to Polar Form of a Phasor Sum
sections.learning_goal: Teach the minimum target: given a rectangular phasor sum $Z = a + jb$, compute $|Z|$ and determine the angle so the resultant sinusoid's amplitude and phase can be read directly from the phasor.

image_policy.image_description_seed: No image needed; the conversion is handled with rectangular components and angle formulas only.
image_policy.image_generation_notes: Keep the section purely symbolic. Do not generate a complex-plane diagram.

question_policy.answer_format: not-applicable
question_policy.practice_question_model: not-applicable

tutorial_outline.direct_instruction_goal: Teach the canonical conversion from rectangular to polar form by identifying $a$ and $b$, computing $|Z| = \sqrt{a^2 + b^2}$, and choosing the correct angle from the sign pattern.
tutorial_outline.base_case: Start with a first-quadrant phasor such as $Z = 4 + 3j$ so the learner sees the magnitude calculation before any quadrant correction.
paragraph_plan: Connect this lesson to the previous rectangular-sum lesson and state that the goal is to turn $Z = a + jb$ into $|Z|\angle\theta$.
Introduce the magnitude formula and explain that the angle depends on the signs of the rectangular components, not on any new frequency information.
Show how the reference angle comes from the component ratio and then gets adjusted to the correct quadrant.
Give one clean positive-quadrant base conversion and point forward to the worked examples that separate magnitude, reference angle, and quadrant choice.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: Not applicable; tutorial section.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Not applicable.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: Not applicable.

sections.handoff_notes: Keep this section compact and symbolic. Introduce magnitude and angle only enough to support the next worked examples; do not convert to the time-domain sinusoid yet.

sections.section_title: Computing the Magnitude of a Rectangular Phasor Sum
sections.learning_goal: Compute the magnitude of a rectangular phasor sum by adding the real and imaginary parts and applying the Euclidean norm.

image_policy.image_description_seed: No image needed; the arithmetic is fully symbolic.
image_policy.image_generation_notes: Keep the worked example and follow-up questions purely symbolic.

question_policy.answer_format: exact magnitude value
question_policy.practice_question_model: Given $Z = (5 + j2) + (1 + j3)$, what is $|Z|$?
distractor_plan: Use $a+b$ instead of $\sqrt{a^2+b^2}$ after finding the rectangular sum.
Square only one component or take the square root too early.
Add absolute values instead of squaring the components.
Make a small arithmetic slip while combining the rectangular parts.

tutorial_outline.direct_instruction_goal: Not applicable; this is a worked example.
tutorial_outline.base_case: Not applicable; this is a worked example.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: Find the magnitude of the rectangular phasor sum $Z = (3 + j4) + (1 + j2)$.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Compute the rectangular sum first and then apply $|Z| = \sqrt{a^2 + b^2}$ to get the resultant magnitude.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: The tutorial established the conversion rule; this example isolates the magnitude computation after the rectangular parts are already known.
solution_step_plan: Add the real parts to get $a$ and the imaginary parts to get $b$.
Apply $|Z| = \sqrt{a^2 + b^2}$.
Simplify the radical to an exact magnitude.
practice_variation_axes: Change one or both component magnitudes while keeping the magnitude formula the same.
Use exact integers or simple surds so the norm is still hand-computable.
Require one small rectangular sum before the magnitude step.

sections.handoff_notes: Anchor this as one-step reinforcement of the symbolic conversion; keep the difficulty low because this is the first worked example after the tutorial.

sections.section_title: Computing the Reference Angle of a Rectangular Phasor Sum
sections.learning_goal: Compute the acute reference angle from rectangular components by using absolute values in the tangent ratio.

image_policy.image_description_seed: No image needed; the reference angle comes directly from the component ratio.
image_policy.image_generation_notes: Keep the conversion symbolic and avoid a coordinate-plane diagram.

question_policy.answer_format: acute reference angle
question_policy.practice_question_model: For $Z = -3 - 4j$, what is the reference angle of $Z$?
distractor_plan: Use the final quadrant-adjusted angle instead of the reference angle.
Reverse the ratio and compute $\tan^{-1}(|a|/|b|)$.
Drop the absolute values and let the signs change the acute angle.
Confuse degrees and radians.

tutorial_outline.direct_instruction_goal: Not applicable; this is a worked example.
tutorial_outline.base_case: Not applicable; this is a worked example.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: From the sum $Z = -4 + 3j$, compute the reference angle.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Use $\theta_{\text{ref}} = \tan^{-1}\!\left(\frac{|b|}{|a|}\right)$ once the sum is in rectangular form.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: This example keeps the same rectangular-sum style but now strips the signs to get the acute reference angle before quadrant adjustment.
solution_step_plan: Read $a$ and $b$ from the rectangular form.
Take the ratio $|b|/|a|$.
Compute the acute reference angle with $\tan^{-1}( |b| / |a| )$.
practice_variation_axes: Swap the signs of $a$ and $b$ while keeping the ratio the same.
Use a quadrant-II or quadrant-III phasor so the signs do not change the reference angle.
Keep the numeric ratio simple enough that the angle is exact.

sections.handoff_notes: Make the reference-angle step explicit and separate from quadrant choice. The student should not yet be asked for the final argument.

sections.section_title: Choosing the Correct Quadrant for the Phasor Angle
sections.learning_goal: Determine the full phase angle by combining the reference angle with the sign pattern of the rectangular components.

image_policy.image_description_seed: No image needed; the sign pattern is enough to determine the quadrant.
image_policy.image_generation_notes: Keep the example rule-based and symbolic. Do not add a quadrant diagram.

question_policy.answer_format: principal phase angle
question_policy.practice_question_model: If $Z = -2 - 2j$, what is $\arg(Z)$?
distractor_plan: Use the reference angle directly without adjusting for quadrant.
Add or subtract the wrong multiple of $\pi$ from the reference angle.
Swap the quadrant-III and quadrant-IV sign rules.
Return a positive coterminal angle when the lesson convention expects a principal angle.

tutorial_outline.direct_instruction_goal: Not applicable; this is a worked example.
tutorial_outline.base_case: Not applicable; this is a worked example.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: For the rectangular phasor $Z = -5 + 12j$, find the quadrant-adjusted phase angle.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Convert the reference angle into the final principal argument by applying the correct sign-based quadrant rule.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: The previous example isolated the reference angle; this one adds the quadrant correction and returns the full phase.
solution_step_plan: Compute the reference angle from $|a|$ and $|b|$.
Identify the signs: $a < 0$ and $b > 0$ put the phasor in quadrant II.
Set $\theta = \pi - \theta_{\text{ref}}$.
practice_variation_axes: Move to quadrant III and IV examples to force different adjustment formulas.
Keep the reference angle exact but vary the sign pattern.
Use the principal-angle convention consistently.

sections.handoff_notes: This section is the error-sensitive gate; include high-quality distractors for sign and quadrant mistakes.

sections.section_title: Writing the Polar Phasor Sum and Reading Its Magnitude and Angle
sections.learning_goal: Write the final phasor in polar form and read its magnitude and angle as the sinusoid's amplitude and phase.

image_policy.image_description_seed: No image needed; the final readout is numerical and symbolic.
image_policy.image_generation_notes: Keep the final conversion symbolic. Do not convert the phasor back into a time-domain sinusoid in this lesson.

question_policy.answer_format: polar magnitude-angle pair
question_policy.practice_question_model: What is the polar form of $Z = -1 - \sqrt{3}j$?
distractor_plan: Keep the magnitude correct but choose the wrong quadrant for the angle.
Use the reference angle $\pi/3$ instead of the signed phase angle.
Swap the magnitude and angle.
Leave the answer in rectangular form instead of polar form.

tutorial_outline.direct_instruction_goal: Not applicable; this is a worked example.
tutorial_outline.base_case: Not applicable; this is a worked example.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: Convert the rectangular phasor sum $Z = 1 - \sqrt{3}j$ into polar form and state the corresponding magnitude and phase.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Produce $Z = 2\angle -\pi/3$ and identify the same magnitude and angle as the sinusoid's amplitude and phase.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: This final step merges the magnitude, reference-angle, and quadrant work into one complete conversion pipeline.
solution_step_plan: Compute $|Z| = 2$ from the rectangular components.
Read the reference angle from the $1 : \sqrt{3}$ ratio as $\pi/3$.
Apply the quadrant-IV sign rule to get $\theta = -\pi/3$.
Write the phasor in polar form and identify the magnitude as amplitude and the angle as phase.
practice_variation_axes: Move the phasor into a different quadrant while keeping a clean exact magnitude.
Vary between exact special angles and non-special arctangent values.
Ask either for polar form only or for the polar form plus amplitude/phase reading.

sections.handoff_notes: Close the lesson by making the readout explicit: magnitude becomes amplitude and angle becomes phase. Do not convert the phasor back into a time-domain sinusoid yet.

entries.lesson_title: Converting a Phasor Sum Back to a Sinusoid
entries.lesson_core_move: Convert a polar phasor sum back into a single same-frequency sinusoid by mapping magnitude to amplitude and angle to phase at the common angular frequency.

sections.section_title: Introduction to Converting a Phasor Sum Back to a Sinusoid
sections.learning_goal: Map a polar phasor $A\angle\phi$ to the same-frequency cosine $A\cos(\omega_0 t + \phi)$ by reading magnitude as amplitude, angle as phase, and keeping the common angular frequency fixed.

image_policy.image_description_seed: No image required; the task is purely symbolic phasor-to-cosine conversion.
image_policy.image_generation_notes: No image generation required.

question_policy.answer_format: not-applicable
question_policy.practice_question_model: not-applicable

tutorial_outline.direct_instruction_goal: State the one-rule conversion from a polar phasor sum to a same-frequency cosine: magnitude becomes amplitude, angle becomes phase, and the angular frequency stays the same.
tutorial_outline.base_case: Start with a phasor like $1\angle 0$ so the learner sees the simplest cosine $\cos(\omega_0 t)$ before any nonzero phase or non-unit magnitude appears.
paragraph_plan: Open by naming the target move: read a polar phasor sum and rewrite it as one cosine at the common angular frequency.
Show the base case $1\angle 0 \leftrightarrow \cos(\omega_0 t)$ so the learner sees the amplitude and phase defaults.
Generalize to $A\angle\phi \leftrightarrow A\cos(\omega_0 t + \phi)$ and point out that the magnitude becomes amplitude while the angle becomes phase.
State that the common angular frequency comes from the surrounding problem and is preserved unchanged in the cosine.
Close by previewing that the next examples will isolate amplitude, phase, frequency, and then the full conversion.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: not-applicable
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: not-applicable
example_outline.variation_from_previous: not-applicable

sections.handoff_notes: Keep the opening explicit and compact. Do not introduce rectangular phasors, vector addition, or any visual diagram; the lesson is only the polar-to-cosine mapping.

sections.section_title: Identifying the Sinusoid Amplitude from Phasor Magnitude
sections.learning_goal: Read the magnitude of a polar phasor sum as the amplitude of the equivalent same-frequency cosine.

image_policy.image_description_seed: No image required; the learner can read the magnitude directly from the phasor notation.
image_policy.image_generation_notes: No image generation required.

question_policy.answer_format: Five symbolic answer choices; one correct amplitude value.
question_policy.practice_question_model: A phasor sum is $7\angle 25^\circ$ at common angular frequency $\omega_0$. Which amplitude should the equivalent cosine use?
distractor_plan: Use the angle value as the amplitude.
Use the negative or reciprocal of the magnitude.
Swap the magnitude and angle.
Add or subtract 1 from the magnitude.
Change the frequency or include extra phase structure in the answer.

tutorial_outline.direct_instruction_goal: not-applicable

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: A phasor sum is $7\angle 25^\circ$ at common angular frequency $\omega_0$. Identify the amplitude of the equivalent same-frequency cosine.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Show that the amplitude is the phasor magnitude, so the cosine uses amplitude $7$.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: This first example isolates the magnitude-to-amplitude mapping while leaving phase and frequency as context rather than the main task.
solution_step_plan: Read the magnitude from the polar phasor.
Match that magnitude to the amplitude of the cosine.
Ignore the angle for this step except to note that it will become phase later.
State the amplitude directly and keep the common angular frequency unchanged.
practice_variation_axes: Change the phasor magnitude.
Use a nonzero angle so the learner does not confuse angle with amplitude.
State the common angular frequency as a named symbol.
Present the phasor as a polar sum already reduced to one term.

sections.handoff_notes: Keep the question generator focused on magnitude only. The distractors should mostly confuse amplitude with angle, sign, reciprocal, or a frequency change.

sections.section_title: Identifying the Sinusoid Phase from Phasor Angle
sections.learning_goal: Read the angle of a polar phasor sum as the phase of the equivalent same-frequency cosine.

image_policy.image_description_seed: No image required; the learner can read the angle directly from the phasor notation.
image_policy.image_generation_notes: No image generation required.

question_policy.answer_format: Five symbolic answer choices; one correct phase value.
question_policy.practice_question_model: A phasor sum is $4\angle -\pi/3$ at common angular frequency $\omega_0$. Which phase should the equivalent cosine use?
distractor_plan: Flip the sign of the angle.
Use the magnitude as the phase.
Mix degrees and radians in the phase value.
Drop the phase entirely and answer with amplitude only.
Change the frequency or write a sine instead of a cosine.

tutorial_outline.direct_instruction_goal: not-applicable

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: A phasor sum is $4\angle -\pi/3$ at common angular frequency $\omega_0$. Identify the phase of the equivalent same-frequency cosine.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Show that the phase is the phasor angle, including its sign, so the cosine uses phase $-\pi/3$.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: This mirrors the amplitude example but now isolates the angle-to-phase mapping instead of the magnitude-to-amplitude mapping.
solution_step_plan: Read the angle from the polar phasor.
Match that angle to the cosine phase.
Preserve the sign of the angle exactly.
Keep the amplitude and common angular frequency unchanged for this step.
practice_variation_axes: Use positive and negative angles.
Use radians or degrees consistently with the prompt.
Include zero phase as a boundary case.
Write the phase as a symbol or a numeric value.

sections.handoff_notes: Keep amplitude fixed and make the only new judgment the angle-to-phase reading. Preserve the sign exactly.

sections.section_title: Preserving the Common Angular Frequency in the Sinusoid

entries.lesson_title: Amplitude-Phase Form of a Sinusoidal Sum
entries.lesson_core_move: Express a same-frequency sinusoidal sum in amplitude-phase form by adding component phasors and converting the resultant magnitude and angle into the combined amplitude and phase.

sections.section_title: Introduction to Amplitude-Phase Form of a Sinusoidal Sum
sections.learning_goal: Introduce amplitude-phase form as the single-cosine result of adding same-frequency phasors and reading the resultant magnitude and angle.
